source.title: Latent-space Attacks for Refusal Evasion in Language Models
source.authors: Giorgio Piras; Raffaele Mura; Fabio Brau; Maura Pintor; Luca Oneto; Fabio Roli; B. Biggio

record.tranche_reason: The study applies DiM refusal-direction ablation as a baseline on new models and reports harmful-request attack success rates. It also benchmarks a multiple-direction method against DiM, but does not test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports separate DiM, MD, and RDO ASRs in Tables 1–2. Probe accuracy figures and CLE results are not included as rows: they do not measure the claimed DiM ablation itself. The paper reports no direction-addition test on harmless requests and no weight-edit or training-against-ablation test.
record.test_reason: The study runs Arditi et al.'s DiM ablation with the official pipeline on 15 models and reports HarmBench ASR. It argues formally and empirically that ablation is a minimum-confidence projection onto a probe boundary, so it often fails to suppress refusal. That is a specific argument, with numbers, that V1 needs restating, so it counts as T5 rather than a plain T1 replication. The measure also differs: a HarmBench classifier, not the original refusal/safety scores. Multi-direction (MD) ablation versus DiM bears on V4. The DiM rows on reasoning models bear on V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that DiM ablation is exactly a projection onto a linear probe's decision boundary, a minimum-confidence (DeepFool-like) evasion that is too weak to reliably suppress refusal. Their margin-controlled CLE attacks, especially the additive CLE-A, reach state-of-the-art ASR across 15 models and beat ablation baselines and GCG/SAA. They say this relies on refused and answered prompts being linearly separable, which held in every model tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means refusal directions and activation ablation as a baseline, following the cited method and official codebase. The paper selects a best direction through its pipeline and evaluates with HarmBench ASR; it does not reproduce every original experiment or measure the original claim’s full set of behavioral effects.
record.method_sensitivity: The DiM attack-success result varies substantially across model/checkpoint; the paper reports this across instruction-tuned, reasoning, and multimodal models. The DiM direction is selected by a pipeline that ranks candidate directions using refusal, steering, and KL-divergence scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-layer SVM-probe directions, pushed past the decision boundary with an optimized margin (CLE-P/CLE-A), reach 85–100% ASR on all 15 models. The same intervention with margin 0 (pure boundary projection) gives near-zero ASR (Fig. 3a, Figs. 4/10/11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing refusal requires moving activations into the compliant region of a linear refusal probe, not just projecting out the refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear SVM probes predict refusal more accurately than DiM probes. DiM AUC is 0.987 on LLaMA2-7B and 0.904 on Mistral-7B-RR; the gap is larger on DeepSeek-R1-8B (Figs. 5–6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The DiM direction is a suboptimal linear separator of refused versus answered prompts.

record.problems: DiM ASR is an indirect measure of refusal removal, and no untreated ASR baseline is provided in Tables 1–2. Capability benchmarks are reported for CLE-P/CLE-A, not for DiM ablation. The study uses HarmBench test prompts and a specified judge; no uncertainty interpretation beyond the reported ± values is stated.

untested.parts: Adding the DiM direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. Capability preservation under DiM ablation (MMLU/ARC/TruthfulQA are reported only for CLE). Untreated ASR baseline.
Direct characterization of refusal geometry (affine, cone dimensionality, dominant-plus-secondary). RDO is reported only as a single best direction.
Effects specific to the reasoning trace; reasoning is not isolated from model family or training.

missing.what: Latent-space evidence that DiM ablation barely moves harmful activations along PC1 toward the harmless cluster. Probe compliance confidence under DiM also stays near the harmful level during generation.
Margin-0 and all-layer boundary-projection ablations (minimum-confidence evasion with SVM or DiM probes) give lowest ASR per model.
No untreated (no-intervention) ASR is reported, so DiM gains cannot be measured against baseline.

record.verdict_notes: The DiM LLaMA2-7B result (1.80 ASR) conflicts sharply with the original paper. It may reflect the direction-selection pipeline, the HarmBench judge, or prompt filtering, and the authors don't investigate. MD and its 7-direction BO selection come from the same authors' prior paper, so tuning effort may favor MD. RDO is reported as a single best direction with ±0.00 and very low ASR, so those rows are unlinked. Capability retention is reported only for CLE, not DiM. Preprint; code release promised.

versions.untested_parts: Adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, and whether DiM ablation preserves general capabilities, are not tested for the DiM intervention.

The study benchmarks multiple-direction and cone-based suppression methods, but does not directly characterize refusal geometry as affine or a cone, or establish a dominant-direction-plus-others representation.
The DiM baseline is tested on several reasoning models, but the study does not isolate reasoning as a causal factor or test every reasoning model.

relation.reason: DiM ablation is run as a baseline and its results (Tables 1 and 2) plus Figs. 1, 8 and 9 are used to argue about whether ablation suppresses refusal. Its own results bear on V1, not merely cited or assumed.

tranche.reason: The paper reruns Arditi et al.'s DiM ablation with the official codebase and default pipeline (T1-like), but its purpose and contribution is the argument, formal and empirical, that ablation is exactly a minimum-confidence boundary projection and therefore the weakest intervention that flips the decision. That is a specific argument with numbers that V1 needs restating, so T5 subsumes T1. The reader's pre-verdict call of T1 is the weaker read.

source_check.notes: All 25 row values, baselines and uncertainties match Tables 1 and 2 exactly. Two condition errors: dim-gptoss and md-gptoss say "reasoning and multimodal", but Table 2 marks GPT-OSS-20B R=yes MM=no (the pack's verdict-fix lines already flag this; the condition fields still need fixing). Neither table has an untreated/no-attack ASR column, so every DiM "partial" vs "observed" state rests on comparison with the paper's other methods, not on a pre-ablation refusal rate; dim-olmo and dim-llama3 are the two states where that choice is genuinely arguable. Capability evidence (MMLU/ARC/TruthfulQA, Tables 4-5) exists only for CLE-P/CLE-A on 7 instruct models, so V1's "other abilities largely kept" and V4 capability retention are untested for DiM and MD here. The verdict labelled V1 challenges on Mistral-7B-RR should be limits_scope: the defended checkpoint is outside V1's stated scope and the failure is expected from the defense.
